questions.question: Why might asking a human to approve every action catch fewer harmful actions than asking less?
options: With many prompts, reviewers stop reading and approve by habit, so the harmful one gets the least attention
It can't; more prompts are always safer
questions.explanation: Approval fatigue turns a check into a habit. Fewer, more meaningful prompts keep attention high.

questions.question: Ask-by-risk-tier never showed the deletion of 40 lines of payment tests. Why?
options: It was classified medium risk and reversible, which that policy doesn't ask about
questions.explanation: Risk tiers judge the kind of action, not whether it was expected. The plan policy caught it as off-plan.

questions.question: How should you treat the attention curve in the simulation?
options: As an assumption; change it and check whether the ranking of policies still holds
As a constant every team shares
questions.explanation: The curve is a model. The lesson is the method: compare policies under different assumptions, then measure your own reviewers.

questions.question: An approval request has been waiting 30 hours with a 24-hour expiry. What happens on 'approve'?
options: Denied: expired approvals default to no
questions.explanation: Silence and delay must fail closed. The agent can ask again with fresh facts.

questions.question: A human approved paying INV-77. Before the agent resumes, the supplier's IBAN on file changes. What should happen?
options: Re-ask: the approval was for the facts the human saw, and their fingerprint no longer matches
questions.explanation: Bind approvals to facts. A changed world needs a new decision.

questions.question: Your logs show a reviewer approving 98% of requests with a median decision time of 0.8 seconds. What does that suggest?
options: The prompts have stopped being a real check; reduce and sharpen them
The reviewer is very fast at reading
questions.explanation: Sub-second, near-universal approval is the signature of fatigue.
